question: The solvent pH has dropped below 6. What does that mean and what do I do?
reference_note: Relabelled 2026-11-13 (iteration 2) from SOP-CO2-SR-01 §8 (pH < 7.0 catalyst deactivation) and design deck p4, p8 (pH < 8 not efficient, go to desorption); the iteration-1 label came from the retired amine drafts.
evidence_lines:
[G1] [G1] Sensor "Solution pH (pH-101)": Solution pH, pH-101. Shows whether the potassium carbonate (K₂CO₃) solvent is still capturing CO₂ and whether desorption is complete (design deck p4, p7–9). (unit: pH)
[G2] [G2] OperatingMode "Absorption": Heater off, pressure raised, pump on: solvent is sprayed from the top while gas enters at the bottom (design deck p8). SOP: PRV-1 3 bar, PRV-2 1 bar, open BV-1 and ABV-1, ABV-2, ABV-5, motor on, set liquid flow on rotameter R2 (SOP-CO2-SR-01 §2A).
[G3] [G3] OperatingMode "Desorption": Solvent at the column base is heated to release CO₂ and regenerate it (design deck p9). SOP: TIC heater 110 °C, ABV-1 and ABV-4 open to send CO₂ out (SOP-CO2-SR-01 §2B).
[G4] [G4] Sensor "CO₂ concentration": Outlet CO₂ concentration from the NDIR analyser at the column gas outlet, read once a second (SOP-CO2-SR-01 §2A; design deck p4). The installed analyser reads 0–2,001 ppm (Lim 2026). (unit: ppm)
[G5] [G5] Sensor "Column temperature (T-101)": Column/bed temperature T-101; it feeds the TIC heater controller (SOP-CO2-SR-01 §8; design deck p7). (unit: °C)
[G6] [G6] Sensor "Column pressure (P-101)": Column pressure P-101, gauge, in barg (SOP-CO2-SR-01 §8). (unit: barg)
[G7] [G7] Threshold "pH < 8" [THIS RIG]: Below pH 8 the solvent is no longer efficient: switch to desorption. Ideal pH is 11–12 (design deck p4, p7–9). The SOP's safe range is 8.5–11.0 (SOP-CO2-SR-01 §8). (operator: <; value: 8.0; unit: pH; applies_mode: None)
[G8] [G8] Threshold "pH < 7.0 (critical)" [THIS RIG]: Critical bound for pH-101: catalyst deactivation (SOP-CO2-SR-01 §8). (operator: <; value: 7.0; unit: pH; applies_mode: None)
[G9] [G9] Threshold "Temperature > 110 °C" [THIS RIG]: Above the 25–110 °C safe range for T-101. During desorption the TIC cuts heater power (SOP-CO2-SR-01 §8–9). (operator: >; value: 110; unit: °C; applies_mode: None)
[G10] [G10] Threshold "Temperature > 120 °C (trip)" [THIS RIG]: Critical trip bound for T-101, runaway risk: emergency shutdown (SOP-CO2-SR-01 §4, §8). (operator: >; value: 120; unit: °C; applies_mode: None)
[G11] [G11] Threshold "Pressure > 3.5 barg" [THIS RIG]: Above the 1.0–3.5 barg safe range for P-101: the software throttles PCV-104 or alerts to open the ABV-4 vent (SOP-CO2-SR-01 §8–9). (operator: >; value: 3.5; unit: barg; applies_mode: None)
[G12] [G12] Threshold "Pressure > 5.0 barg (trip)" [THIS RIG]: Critical trip bound for P-101: emergency shutdown (SOP-CO2-SR-01 §4, §8). The design is kept at 1 bar, max 5 bar (design deck p4, p6). (operator: >; value: 5.0; unit: barg; applies_mode: None)
[G13] [G13] OperatingMode "Manual": If automated sequences hang, the operator toggles ABV-1 to ABV-5 directly from the dashboard (SOP-CO2-SR-01 §3).
answer:
The solvent pH has dropped below 6, which is below the safe operating range of 8.5 to 11.0. This indicates that the potass0ium carbonate solvent is no longer efficient at capturing CO₂. As per the standard operating procedure (SOP) for this reactor, when the pH falls below 8, the system should switch to desorption mode. ⟦removed⟧

To address this issue, you should manually switch the operating mode to "Desorption" by toggling ABV-1 to ABV-5 directly from the dashboard, as per the SOP-CO2-SR-01 §3. This will initiate the desorption process, where the solvent at the column base is heated to release CO₂ and regenerate it.

Additionally, it's important to monitor the solvent pH closely to prevent it from dropping further and to ensure the efficiency of the CO2 capture process. If the pH continues to drop, it may be necessary to investigate potential issues with the solvent or the reactor system.

To calibrate a gas chromatograph, you typically follow these steps:

1. Prepare calibration standards: You need to prepare solutions with known concentrations of the analyte you want to measure. These standards should cover the expected concentration range of your samples.

2. Set up the gas chromatograph: Make sure the instrument is clean and in good working condition. Check the flow rates of the carrier gas, the oven temperature, and the detector settings.

3. Inject the calibration standards: Inject the calibration standards into the gas chromatograph one at a time, starting with the lowest concentration and working your way up to the highest. Record the peak areas or heights for each standard.

4. Create a calibration curve: Plot the peak areas or heights against the known concentrations of the calibration standards. Fit a linear or non-linear regression model to the data, depending on the relationship between concentration and response.

5. Determine the calibration equation: Calculate the equation of the best-fit line or curve. This equation will be used to convert the peak areas or heights of unknown samples into concentrations.

6. Validate the calibration: Test the calibration by analyzing samples with known concentrations that were not used to create the calibration curve. Compare the calculated concentrations with the actual concentrations to assess the accuracy and precision of the calibration.

7. Apply the calibration: Once the calibration is validated, you can use the calibration equation to determine the concentrations of analytes in your unknown samples.

Remember, the specifics of gas chromatograph calibration may vary depending on the type of detector, the analyte, and the instrument used. Always refer to the instrument's manual and relevant standard operating procedures for detailed instructions.

**What to check:**

4. **pH levels**: Confirm the pH (pH-101) is within the optimal range (typically 8–10) to ensure effective CO₂ capture.
